clinicalPearls: WHO grade 1 sellar/suprasellar epithelial tumour occurring almost exclusively in adults, in contrast to the bimodal age distribution of the adamantinomatous type.
Nearly all cases harbour the BRAF V600E mutation, whereas adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma is driven by CTNNB1 (beta-catenin/Wnt) mutations.
Typically a well-circumscribed, often solid or mixed suprasellar or third-ventricular mass with less calcification than the adamantinomatous type.
Histology shows well-differentiated non-keratinising squamous epithelium arranged in papillae over fibrovascular cores, lacking wet keratin, peripheral palisading and stellate reticulum.
Presents with visual field loss (classically bitemporal hemianopia), headache, hypopituitarism and sometimes diabetes insipidus or hypothalamic dysfunction.
BRAF inhibition, usually combined with MEK inhibition, can produce marked tumour shrinkage and is an emerging neoadjuvant or adjuvant option.
Endocrine and visual assessment are essential before and after treatment given the parasellar location.
Sparse calcification and a predominantly solid appearance in an adult favour the papillary over the adamantinomatous type.
reference.pathophysiology: Papillary craniopharyngioma is a benign epithelial tumour of the sellar and suprasellar region, thought to arise from metaplasia of adenohypophyseal epithelial cells or ectodermal remnants, and is molecularly defined by the near-universal presence of the activating BRAF V600E mutation with resultant constitutive MAPK/ERK pathway signalling. This contrasts sharply with adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, which is driven by activating CTNNB1 mutations and aberrant Wnt/beta-catenin signalling with nuclear beta-catenin accumulation. Histologically it forms papillae of mature, well-differentiated non-keratinising squamous epithelium over fibrovascular cores and lacks the wet keratin, peripheral palisading, stellate reticulum and dystrophic calcification typical of the adamantinomatous variant. Its location adjacent to the optic chiasm, pituitary and hypothalamus accounts for the visual, endocrine and hypothalamic manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Germinoma or other germ cell tumour
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the sella and suprasellar region to define the solid/cystic mass and its relation to the chiasm, pituitary and third ventricle
CT to assess calcification (usually sparse in the papillary type) and the bony sella
Full anterior pituitary hormone profile and assessment for diabetes insipidus using paired serum and urine osmolality
Formal visual acuity, colour vision and perimetry (visual field) testing
Histopathology with BRAF V600E testing by immunohistochemistry and/or molecular assay
Ophthalmology and endocrinology review, including fundoscopy
redFlags: Rapidly progressive visual loss or a new visual field defect
Features of hypopituitarism or adrenal insufficiency, such as fatigue, hypotension or hyponatraemia
Polyuria and polydipsia suggesting diabetes insipidus, particularly in the perioperative period
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus from third-ventricular obstruction
Acute hypothalamic disturbance affecting temperature, appetite or conscious level
reference.prognosis: Generally favourable for a WHO grade 1 tumour, with complete resection often curative and recurrence rates tending to be lower than for the adamantinomatous type. The parasellar location can nonetheless leave lasting visual or endocrine morbidity, and BRAF-targeted therapy offers effective disease control in selected cases.
pitfalls: Assuming all craniopharyngiomas are alike; failing to test for BRAF V600E misses a targeted-therapy opportunity specific to the papillary type.
Overlooking or undertreating perioperative endocrine deficits, particularly cortisol deficiency and diabetes insipidus.
Mistaking a solid enhancing papillary craniopharyngioma for a pituitary macroadenoma or a meningioma.
Pursuing aggressive complete resection when the tumour is adherent, risking hypothalamic injury.
